paragraphs.text: Fix the 300s undici bodyTimeout that kills long LLM SSE streams with TypeError: terminated (DeepSeek
Harness host plugin)
# dsh-stream-timeout-fix
**English** · 简体中文

A tiny **DeepSeek Harness (DSH)** host plugin that stops Node's built-in `fetch`
from killing long,
silently-stalled LLM streams — the ones that die with
[代码示例省略，未执行]

after roughly 304–305 seconds of mid-stream silence, and get reported as a
`TRANSPORT` failure even
though the provider never hung up.

> **Who this is for.** Third-party / self-hosted OpenAI-compatible endpoints whose
> responses can t

ake a long time and occasionally stall mid-stream: university or
> company private deployments, Lite

LLM-style gateways, self-hosted vLLM, and the
> like. Against a well-behaved large cloud API you pro

bably do not need it.
>
> **Maintenance.** Written by the author for personal use, and published in

case it
> helps someone else. It may not be actively maintained, issues and PRs may go
> unanswered,

and there is no support commitment. The plugin is ~120 lines — read it
> before you install it. See

**Validation status** below: the fix is confirmed by a real
> 607 s silence that survived end-to-en

d.
>
> **Distribution.** There is no npm package — this is a small single-purpose patch and
> does n
ot warrant one. Install straight from this repository; see Install.
## The symptom
With a streaming LLM endpoint, some requests fail like this:

* the SSE response is **already established and content has started flowing**
(reasoning tokens, par

tial answers, tool-call deltas), then
* **nothing arrives for minutes** while the upstream keeps gen

erating, and then
* the request dies locally after ~304–305 s of silence with
`TypeError: terminated
`, classified as a transport/network error.

The provider's own logs show the opposite of a provider-side failure: it records a
**client disconne

ct** (LiteLLM / nginx log `499`) and the upstream **still finishes
generating and still bills the to
kens** — you pay for output you never received.
## The root cause

Node's built-in `fetch` runs on undici, which
ships two client-side clocks that are invisible until

lt-in `fetch` runs on undici, which
ships two client-side clocks that are invisible until they fire:
| Clock | Default | Applies to | Error when it fires |
| `headersTimeout` | `300_000 ms` | waiting for the first response byte | `TypeError: fetch failed`,

cause `HeadersTimeoutError` (`UND_ERR_HEADERS_TIMEOUT`) |
| `bodyTimeout` | `300_000 ms` | idle gap
**between body bytes** (re-armed by every received byte) | `TypeError: terminated`, cause `BodyTime
outError` (`UND_ERR_BODY_TIMEOUT`) |

Because `bodyTimeout` is re-armed per byte, ordinary slow-but-flowing streams are
never affected (st

reams running 20+ minutes are fine). It only bites when the
**gap** exceeds 300 s — exactly what a s
talled upstream produces.
Two things make this hard to attribute correctly:

1. `bodyTimeout` reports itself as **`terminated`**, i.e. literally "the other side
[该节后续省略]
## What this plugin does

DSH's LLM path never passes a custom `fetch`
(`dsh-llm-pi-ai` → `pi-ai` → OpenAI SDK v6 → `globalThi

s.fetch` → **global undici
dispatcher**), so one process-wide swap covers every provider at once:
[代码示例省略，未执行]

* `bodyTimeout = 30 min`, `headersTimeout = 10 min` by default — finite on purpose,
so a genuinely d

ead peer is still reclaimed.
* Stream-level watchdogs (e.g. pi-ai's `streamIdleTimeoutMs`) and provi

der retry
policies remain the real guards; this plugin only removes the *disagreement*
between two i

dle clocks.
* Cross-version injection is fine: the global dispatcher lives in a process-wide
`Symbol

.for('undici.globalDispatcher.1')` slot, so an `Agent` created by undici
8.x is honored by Node's bu
ilt-in `fetch` (undici 7.x).
## What this plugin does not do

* **No retries.** It ships no retry policy and never re-sends a request. Retrying is
the job of DSH'

s own retry plugin (`@deepseek-ai/dsh-llm-retry`), configured per
provider in your profile patch — s

ee the pairing section below if you want both.
* **No provider, auth or routing configuration.** It

mounts no service, registers no
tool, and touches no endpoint or credential.
* **No cost control.**

It cannot cap, cancel or budget anything — read the next section.
* **No server-side change.** If yo

ur gateway has its own idle-connection limit, this
plugin will not help; ask your operator for SSE c

omment heartbeats instead.
* **No change to DSH's own stream watchdog.** `streamIdleTimeoutMs` is pe

r-route
configuration (`dsh-llm-pi-ai`), not something a dispatcher swap can touch — see
“Raise `str
eamIdleTimeoutMs` as well”.
## Scope and caveats

* **Process-wide by design.** Every `fetch` in the DSH host process (all
providers, other plugins) l

oses the 300 s default ceiling and inherits the
configured one. That is the point, but it is a real

blast radius.
* **Cross-version dispatcher reports are tested, not assumed.** Several upstream
discu

ssions (`#7721`, `#7671`, `#7598`, `#7468`, `#7502`) blame a *userland*
undici 8.x dispatcher in the

process-global slot for breaking content-encoding and
response headers on Node's built-in fetch (bu

ndled undici 7.x) — the same slot
this plugin swaps. `scripts/check-content-encoding.mjs` (part of `

npm test`)
verifies gzip decoding **before and after** the swap; it passes on Node 24.21 with
undici

8.11.2. If you ever see raw gzip/brotli or missing headers after
installing, disable the plugin and

report your `node -v` plus
`process.versions.undici` pair.
* **Not a cure for upstream stalls.** If

your provider pauses for minutes, the
request still takes minutes. Pair this with a retry policy, a

nd prefer smaller
outputs so a stall costs less.
* **Client-side keepalive is not an option.** After

an HTTP/1.1 POST body is sent,
a client has no legal place to write on that request, and SSE is one

-way
(server → client). TCP keepalive and HTTP/2 PINGs only address transport-idle
middleboxes. The

only legitimate in-stream heartbeat is a **server-sent SSE
comment** (`: ping`) — a server-side meas

ure. This plugin is the client-side fix.
* Node only. It has no effect on Python/Go/Rust clients, wh

ich do not ship this
default (a useful hint when a colleague "can run 700 s requests" and you cannot

h do not ship this
default (a useful hint when a colleague "can run 700 s requests" and you cannot).
